extracted.intended_audience: researchers and conference organizers designing or evaluating reviewer-assignment algorithms (peer-review / program chairs / algorithm designers)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and design criteria for conference reviewer-assignment algorithms: measuring fairness, total sum similarity, runtime, and downstream decision accuracy; and constraints (loads, conflicts) that assignments must satisfy. Used to compare algorithms (PeerReview4All, TPMS, ILPR, FairIr, FairFlow, AHARD, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness ΓS(A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The fairness metric ΓS(A) (referred to as (3) in the paper) that captures the quality received by the worst-off papers under assignment A; used as the primary objective of PeerReview4All (algorithm aims at optimizing fairness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness guarantees of Theorem 1 are achieved after the first iteration of Steps 2 to 7; subsequent iterations improve fairness for the next worst-off papers. PeerReview4All significantly increases fairness compared to TPMS; FairIr and ILPR have related fairness guarantees (may become vacuous under heterogeneous similarity). Fairness can be lower-bounded/upper-bounded analytically (used to derive approximation guarantees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Total (cumulative / mean) sum similarity GS(A)
rubrics_metrics.description: The total (or mean) sum of similarities of assigned reviewer-paper pairs (referred to as (2) or GS(A)); a conventional objective measuring overall match quality of an assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PeerReview4All does not directly optimize GS(A) but can heuristically improve it via the max-cost heuristic in Step 6. There is a tradeoff between maximizing fairness and maximizing sum similarity; algorithms are compared on both axes. Table 3/4 report mean sum similarity; higher values indicate better global match quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Running time / computational feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Wall-clock running time of the assignment algorithm (seconds reported in experiments), and computational scalability to large instances (number of papers/reviewers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PeerReview4All's naive implementation is significantly slower than competitors; for large instances often only a single iteration is feasible. Nevertheless, first iteration suffices for fairness guarantees. Example: first iteration on >5,000 papers took under three hours, which is feasible in conference timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitiveness (normalized fairness and sum-similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Per-experiment normalization: competitiveness in fairness = (fairness achieved by algorithm)/(max fairness across algorithms); similarly for total sum similarity. Each algorithm is represented as a point in 2D (fairness competitiveness, sum-similarity competitiveness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closeness of the point to the top-right corner indicates superior joint performance on fairness and sum similarity. Used to visualize and compare tradeoffs across algorithms and conferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy of final decisions (error fraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraction of papers/questions whose final estimated decisions (accept/reject or answer) are incorrect under the assignment and aggregation procedure (e.g., majority vote). In MTurk experiment this is the fraction of questions whose final answers are estimated incorrectly; ties counted as mistakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to directly measure downstream impact of assignments on decision accuracy. Observed that AHARD (optimally fair) can incur larger error fraction than approximations (APR4A, AILPR) because maximizing the worst-off paper can hurt global accuracy. TPMS showed increased error versus APR4A in MTurk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility constraints: paper/reviewer load (λ, μ)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard assignment feasibility constraints: each paper must be assigned exactly λ reviewers and each reviewer can review at most μ papers (and possibly lower/upper bounds). Assignments must respect these load constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments and theoretical bounds assume these constraints. Some competing algorithms (FairIr, FairFlow) optionally allow specifying a lower bound on reviewer load (ensuring each reviewer reviews at least some number of papers); PeerReview4All as described does not enforce reviewer lower-bound constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-conflict constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments must ensure that no paper is assigned to a conflicting reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In experiments the authors require that no paper is assigned to any conflicting reviewer in addition to load constraints; conflicts are filtered out before matching (standard operational constraint in conference peer-review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation ratio relative to AHARD (theoretical guarantee)
rubrics_metrics.description: The worst-case approximation guarantee of PeerReview4All compared to the optimal fairness assignment AHARD: ΓS(APR4A)/ΓS(AHARD) ≥ 1/λ (Theorem 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice the approximation factor can be much better than the worst-case bound (e.g., empirical lower bound ≥ 0.98 on ICLR’18 similarity matrix when dropping reviewer loads). The proof uses bounds on s*_κ and monotonicity of transformation functions f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Max-cost heuristic selection (design/heuristic criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of heuristic in Step 6 (max-cost heuristic) when multiple suitable similarity matrices are available; used to heuristically optimize total sum similarity while preserving fairness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the max-cost heuristic helps PeerReview4All maintain high cumulative similarity, keeping GS(A) only marginally below optimal while achieving higher fairness. Heuristic choice is an explicit design lever to balance objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early-stopping / iteration sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical and theoretical observation that fairness guarantees can be achieved after a single iteration of Steps 2–7; further iterations improve fairness for subsequent worst-off papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For large instances computing only the first iteration is feasible and sufficient to obtain the fairness guarantee of Theorem 1; additional iterations refine assignment for more papers (e.g., second worst-off, third worst-off).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between fairness and total sum similarity (multi-objective desideratum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Desideratum that an assignment algorithm should achieve a good tradeoff between improving quality for worst-off papers (fairness) and maintaining high overall match quality (sum similarity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PeerReview4All explicitly targets fairness but can be tuned (via heuristics) to maintain high sum similarity. Comparative experiments evaluate algorithms on both axes; an ideal algorithm would be simultaneously competitive on both metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lower bound on reviewer load as a capability (optional constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some algorithms (FairIr, FairFlow) allow specifying a lower bound on reviewer load to ensure each reviewer reviews at least some number of papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a design/constraints difference between algorithms; PeerReview4All does not support lower bounds on reviewer load 'as is' in the presented work, so comparisons excluded instances where lower bounds were enforced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-paper (ordered) sum-similarity and worst-off paper analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Per-paper analysis: compute sum similarity for each paper, sort papers by increasing sum similarity, plot values for the most disadvantaged papers (e.g., 100 worst-off) and plot ratios (PeerReview4All to TPMS) across ordered papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to show how PeerReview4All improves quality for worst-off papers while decreasing quality for best-off papers; helps visualize balance and distributional effects across papers rather than only aggregate means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical evaluation protocol for objective accuracy measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Design of an experiment (MTurk) to obtain ground-truth-like conditions: define gold-standard questions, compute similarities from gold answers, execute multiple assignment algorithms under identical constraints, aggregate assigned reviewers' answers (majority vote), and measure decision error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a reproducible methodology to evaluate how assignment algorithms affect final decision accuracy. Includes details: split questions into gold/unresolved sets, compute similarities as fraction correct on gold, choose n workers uniformly at random, enforce λ and μ, iterate many times to average results; ties treated as mistakes.
